title: Defining a Cell Type
intro: There is no single agreed definition of a neuron type. Neuroscientists sort cells by their shape, by how they fire, by which genes they express and by what they connect to. The modern view is that a type is a cluster that stays consistent across several of these at once, and large atlases now measure all of them in the same cells.

items: Morphology (m-type): the shape of the dendrites and axon. Pyramidal versus stellate, where the apical dendrite ends, which layer the axon targets, whether an interneuron's axon wraps somata (basket), axon initial segments (chandelier) or climbs to layer 1 (Martinotti). Measured by filling a cell with dye or biocytin and reconstructing it in 3D.

Electrophysiology (e-type): how the cell responds to injected current. Spike width, firing rate, adaptation, bursting, rebound spikes, sag from the h-current, resonance. Measured with whole-cell patch clamp, usually with standard current steps and ramps.

Molecular or transcriptomic (t-type): which genes the cell expresses. Classic markers such as parvalbumin (PV), somatostatin (SST) and VIP; now whole-transcriptome single-cell RNA sequencing, which in mouse cortex separates over a hundred types (Tasic et al. 2018).

Connectivity and projection: which cells it receives from and where its axon goes. Intratelencephalic, pyramidal-tract and corticothalamic pyramidal cells look similar locally but project to different targets. Connectomics from electron microscopy (for example the MICrONS cubic millimetre of mouse visual cortex) now measures this directly.

blocks.text: Agreement and disagreement between the views

The views agree at the top level. The excitatory versus inhibitory split, and within cortical interneurons the PV, SST and 5HT3aR (including VIP) families, appear in every kind of data. Below that the boundaries blur: a transcriptomic type often maps to a small range of shapes and firing patterns rather than one, and some properties vary continuously along a gradient instead of forming clean clusters. Patch-seq, which records a cell's firing, fills it for morphology and sequences its RNA from the same pipette, was built to test how well the views line up. Gouwens et al. (2020) used it on over 4,000 mouse visual cortex interneurons and found 28 'met-types' consistent across morphology, electrophysiology and transcriptomics.

items: Petilla terminology (Petilla Interneuron Nomenclature Group, Ascoli et al. 2008): a shared vocabulary for interneuron morphology, molecular markers and firing, so 'fast-spiking', 'adapting' and 'stuttering' mean the same in every lab.

Blue Brain m-types and e-types (Markram et al. 2015): 55 morphological types (such as L5_TTPC1, a layer 5 thick-tufted pyramidal cell, or L23_LBC, a layer 2/3 large basket cell) crossed with 11 electrical types (such as cAD continuous adapting, bAC burst accommodating, cNAC continuous non-accommodating), giving 207 morpho-electrical combinations in their juvenile rat somatosensory column.
Allen Institute types: transcriptomic names built from layer, marker genes and projection (for example 'L5 PT' or 'Sst Calb2 Pdlim5'), linked to e-types and m-types through Patch-seq.
Projection classes for pyramidal cells: IT (intratelencephalic), PT or ET (pyramidal-tract or extratelencephalic) and CT (corticothalamic), with NP (near-projecting) and L6b as smaller groups.
Allen Cell Types Database: patch-clamp recordings, morphologies and fitted models (GLIF point models and biophysical models) for mouse and human cortical neurons, freely downloadable.

BICCN / BICAN (BRAIN Initiative Cell Census and Atlas Network): whole-brain transcriptomic atlases of mouse, and growing human and primate atlases; the 2023 mouse whole-brain atlas lists over 5,000 transcriptomic clusters (Yao et al. 2023).
NeuroMorpho.Org: tens of thousands of reconstructed neuron morphologies from many species and labs.
Hippocampome.org: a knowledge base of rodent hippocampal neuron types (over 120) with their morphology, markers, firing and Izhikevich model parameters for each.
Blue Brain Project data: the m-types, e-types, connection rules and models of the rat somatosensory microcircuit.

blocks.text: What this means for a model

A model rarely needs a hundred types. What it needs is one representative per functional role that its question depends on. For a cortical column that is usually an excitatory population per layer plus PV, SST and VIP interneurons; Billeh et al. (2020), the Allen Institute's model of mouse V1, used 17 cell classes. The atlases are useful because they let you pick parameters for each representative from real data (Hippocampome.org and the Allen Cell Types Database both give fitted model parameters per type) rather than inventing them.
